questions.question: Explain how to calculate Target Heart Rate (THR) with an example. / [CO6]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain how to calculate Target Heart Rate (THR) with an example.
  • Target Heart Rate (THR) is the optimal range of heartbeats per minute
  • (bpm) during exercise that ensures the body is working hard enough to
  • gain cardiovascular benefits, but not so hard as to cause strain or
  • overexertion.
  • Formula for Target Heart Rate
  • There are two commonly used methods:
  • Basic Formula:
  • THR = (Maximum Heart Rate × Desired Intensity %)
  • Karvonen Formula (more accurate):
  • THR = [(220 − Age) − Resting Heart Rate] × Intensity + Resting Heart
  • Rate
  • Example Calculation : For a 20-year-old individual, (Students may write
  • any example and use any formula. The one given below is just an example
  • using the basic formula.)
  • Basic formula : THR = Maximum Heart Rate × Desired Intensity%
  • Maximum Heart Rate = 220 − Age
  • Maximum HR = 220 − 20 = 200 bpm.
  • • 50%: 200 × 0.50 = 100 bpm
  • • 60%: 200 × 0.60 = 120 bpm
  • • 70%: 200 × 0.70 = 140 bpm
  • • 80%: 200 × 0.80 = 160 bpm
  • • 90%: 200 × 0.90 = 180 bpm
  • [A] / [CO6]

questions.question: A male college student weighs 72 kg and is 1.68 m tall. Find the student’s BMI and classify the weight status . / [CO6]
questions.solution_html:
• A male college student weighs 72 kg and is 1.68 m tall. Find the student’s BMI and
  • classify the weight status. [A] / [CO6]
  • Formula:
  • BMI=Height2 (m)Body Weight (kg)
  • Calculation:
  • BMI=(1.68)272 BMI=2.822472=25.51 kg/m2
  • BMI = 25.5 kg/m²
  • Classification (WHO adult classification):
  • ● Below 18.5 – Underweight
  • ● 18.5–24.9 – Normal weight
  • ● 25.0–29.9 – Overweight
  • ● 30.0 and above – Obesity
  • Answer: The student's BMI is 25.5 kg/m², which falls under the overweight category.
  • Marking scheme (5 marks):
  • ● Correct formula – 1 mark
  • ● Correct substitution – 1 mark
  • ● Correct calculation – 1 mark
  • ● Correct BMI value – 1 mark
  • ● Correct classification – 1 mark

questions.question: Explain the role of physical inactivity in causing obesity / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the role of physical inactivity in causing obesity
  • Physical inactivity plays a major role in the development of obesity.
  • When a person does not engage in sufficient physical activity, fewer
  • calories are burned, leading to an energy imbalance where calorie intake
  • exceeds expenditure. This excess energy is stored in the body as fat.
  • Inactivity also slows down metabolism and promotes the accumulation
  • of visceral fat, which surrounds vital organs and contributes to serious
  • health risks. Moreover, a sedentary lifestyle leads to muscle loss, which
  • further reduces energy expenditure and increases fat storage. Over time,
  • this cycle contributes to obesity and increases the risk of associated
  • lifestyle diseases such as diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease.
  • Regular physical activity is therefore essential for maintaining a healthy
  • weight and overall well-being.
  • [U] / [CO2]

questions.question: Differentiate between normal bone density, osteopenia, osteoporosis, and severe osteoporosis. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate between normal bone density, osteopenia, osteoporosis, and
  • severe osteoporosis.
  • Bone density reflects the strength and mineral content of bones, which
  • determine their resistance to fractures. Normal bone density refers to
  • healthy bones with a T -score of -1.0 or above, indicating adequate bone
  • strength. Osteopenia occurs when bone density begins to decrease
  • slightly, with a T -score between -1.0 and -2.5. It represents an early
  • warning stage where bones start to lose minerals and become weaker.
  • Osteoporosis is a more advanced condition, defined by a T -score of -2.5
  • or below, where bone loss becomes significant and the risk of fractur es
  • increases. Severe osteoporosis occurs when the T -score is -2.5 or below
  • along with one or more fractures, indicating extreme fragility.
  • Maintaining bone health through regular weight -bearing exercises,
  • sufficient calcium and vitamin D intake, and an act ive lifestyle can help
  • prevent osteoporosis and maintain bone strength throughout life.
  • [U] / [CO3]

questions.question: What are psychosomatic disorders, and how do stress, anxiety, and strong emotions contribute to their development? / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• What are psychosomatic disorders, and how do stress, anxiety, and strong
  • emotions contribute to their development?
  • Psychosomatic disorders are physical illnesses caused by mental or
  • emotional stress. The word psychosomatic means a connection between
  • the mind and body. In these disorders, emotional problems show up as
  • physical symptoms.
  • These are not imaginary—the symptoms are real and can affect daily life.
  • Common examples include headache, ulcers, back pain, asthma, and high
  • blood pressure. Stress is one of the main causes of psychosomatic
  • disorders. When a person is stressed, the brain releases stress hormones
  • like ad renaline and cortisol. These hormones increase heart rate, blood
  • pressure, and muscle tension. Long -term stress can lead to chronic
  • diseases such as hypertension and heart problems. Anxiety also
  • contributes by keeping the body in a constant “alert” state. People with
  • anxiety may feel chest tightness, stomach upset, or dizziness. Strong
  • emotions like anger, sadness, or fear can disturb normal body functions.
  • Suppressed emotions may cause fatigue, digestive issues, or skin
  • [U] / [CO4]
  • problems. Managing stress through yo ga, meditation, or exercise can
  • reduce symptoms. A healthy lifestyle, proper sleep, balanced diet, and
  • emotional support help prevent psychosomatic disorders.
